summary_excerpt: 私たちは現代社会のあらゆる場面で、話しことばの音声を聞いたり発したりして生......
subtitle: 話しことばと現代社会（２）
summary:
私たちは現代社会のあらゆる場面で、話しことばの音声を聞いたり発したりして生活しています。
たとえば、授業中の先生の話、講演会、友人や家族との様々な場所・場面での会話、電話やオンラインツールを用いた会話、駅や電車のアナウンス、店員との会話、政治家のスピーチや討論、選挙演説、ニュース音声、オリンピックなどのスポーツ解説、スポーツ選手のコメント、テレビ番組や映画での会話、漫才の対話、アニメの声、詩の朗読、様々な方言、外国語の音声など。また、話しことばに近いものとしては、ＳＮＳでのチャットやスタンプ、絵文字などがあります。
話しことばの音声は、言語的な情報を伝達するだけでなく、話し手の感情やニュアンスや発話意図なども伝達します。
話しことばの音声は、皆さんの専門分野である政治学や経済学をはじめ、様々な学問領域とも密接に結びついています。
この演習では、以上挙げたような現代社会における話しことばに着目した研究を行います。
話しことばを科学的に研究する学問は音声学と言われます。
母音や子音などの個々の音のみならず、発話全体に関わるイントネーション、アクセント、リズム、話速、ポーズ（休止）といった事柄も扱われます。
この演習では、参加者の関心に沿った研究テーマを設定するにあたり、まずはじめに音声学的な基礎を身に着け、話しことばの音声を科学的に分析する手法を学びます。
その後、参加者の関心あるテーマに関する文献を読みながら、研究テーマを見つけ、最終的には話しことばに関する研究論文を執筆するための準備作業を行います。

summary_excerpt: 私たちの社会を作り上げているものはそのメンバーの間のコミュニケーションです......
subtitle: コミュニケーションとことば
summary:
私たちの社会を作り上げているものはそのメンバーの間のコミュニケーションです。もちろんコミュニケーションにはさまざまな種類のものがありますが、ここで取り上げるのは、ことばによるコミュニケーションです。しかしこれらとの関連で、異なるタイプのコミュニケーション（たとえばノンヴァーバルコミュニケーション）につい考えることもできます。
参加者は自分の問題意識に従って研究テーマを設定することができます。たとえば、さまざまなタイプのコミュニケーションにおけることばの働き、言語のヴァリエーション（地域的変種、社会的変種など）、社会とことば、言語政策、対人関係のことば、異文化コミュニケーション、などが考えられます。授業では、それぞれの問題意識に沿って、どのようなアプローチがありうるのか、先行研究には何があるのかなどを案内しながら、考えます。演習ですから、学生の発表とディスカッションを中心に進めて行きます。
あらゆるコミュニケーション形態の基礎となっているのは個人の間のコミュニケーションです。そこにおけることばの働きについては、語用論 (Pragmatics) と呼ばれる言語学の一分野での研究を知ることが不可欠です。授業ではその主要な理論や分析方法についての導入も行います。また必要に応じてことばの働きそのものについての紹介もします。
goal:
1. コミュニケーションとことばについて自覚的になり、自らのコミュニケーションを反省的に見、改善につなげる試みが行えるようにすること。
2. コミュニケーションに関わるファクターと、それらの働きについて知ることで、他者のコミュニケーションを理解する能力を高めること。
以上2点が本演習の I から IV を通して学修することによって到達する目標です。最終学期であるIV では、IIIまでの調査研究の集大成としての論文作成ををおこないます。その結果としてコミュニケーションに対する高度な感覚と分析手法の評価を行う能力が身につくことを期待します。

teacher: ブロッソー　シルヴィ
summary_excerpt: 本セミナーは、映画の分析（映画研究、映画学）の入門講座である。 映画はシ......
subtitle: 映画研究演習、映画学入門の演習
summary:
本セミナーは、映画の分析（映画研究、映画学）の入門講座である。
映画はショーであり、楽しみをもたらすものだが、研究の対象ともなりうるものである。
映画は、娯楽のために鑑賞することがほとんどである。映画鑑賞は、いわば「感覚の時」とも言え、感動、恐怖、喜び、悲しみ、不安、動揺などを体験する時間である。また映画は、ある話、テーマ、（フィクション上または実在の）人物を、（自然または人工的に作り上げられた）特有の空間において発見する機会であり、知られざる運命や状況、世界に出会う手段である。映画は、画像と同じく、世界の一つの表象である。したがって、映画鑑賞は、我々のいる世界、状況、社会について考える機会となる。映画が、常に世界の表象である、としたら、それをどのように読み解けばよいのだろう。またその表象をどのように描写し、理解し、解釈すればよいのだろう。映画の分析は、これらの質問（何が？どのように？なぜ？）に答えてくれる。映画を分析することで、より多くのことが理解でき、より多くの知識が得られ、より多くのことに関心が持てるようになる。
本セミナーでは、ジャン＝リュック・ゴダールの映画を紹介し、研究する。具体的な例を用いて、映画分析を構成する要素について学ぶ。日本語字幕付きの複数の映画を鑑賞し、その一部について詳しく分析する。映画はかならず意味とメッセージを持ち、時にはイデオロギーをも持つ。映画は型にはまった考え方を見せることもあれば、逆に新たな考えや予想外のイメージを見せることもある。どのように、内容と形式の間の関係を見つけるか？映画内での、話、メッセージと美学の間の関係はどのようなものか？ある映画について、歴史的、社会学的、美学的に興味深い点はどこか？一部のイメージについて、興味深い点はどこか？そうしたイメージは、どのような技術と、どのような構成を用いて組織されているか？面白い部分、重要な部分、意味深い部分はなにか？こうした問題に注目する。
goal:
本セミナーでは、ジャン＝リュック・ゴダールの映画を紹介し、研究する。
具体的な例を用いて、映画分析を構成する要素について学ぶ。
日本語字幕付きの複数の映画を鑑賞し、その一部について詳しく分析する。
映画はかならず意味とメッセージを持ち、時にはイデオロギーをも持つ。
映画は型にはまった考え方を見せることもあれば、逆に新たな考えや予想外のイメージを見せることもある。
どのように、内容と形式の間の関係を見つけるか？
映画内での、話、メッセージと美学の間の関係はどのようなものか？
ある映画について、歴史的、社会学的、美学的に興味深い点はどこか？
一部のイメージについて、興味深い点はどこか？そうしたイメージは、どのような技術と、どのような構成を用いて組織されているか？
面白い部分、重要な部分、意味深い部分はなにか？こうした問題に注目する。
study_outside:
本セミナーでは、ジャン＝リュック・ゴダールの映画を紹介し、研究する。
本セミナーにおいては、特に背景、セット、そして空間と風景の表象、すなわち映画に現れる場所、風景、そこに用いられた光、色彩といった要素に注目する。アクションが起こる場所はどこか？こうした空間の劇的な機能はどこにあるのか？映画の中、フィクションの中、話の中における風景の役割はどのようなものか？風景は、映画の話や、人物、時間、空間を設定するための単なる背景としてだけ存在するのではない。風景は、ある雰囲気・環境や、感情をもたらすほか、様々な意味、レフェランス（ほかの芸術作品の暗示など）、象徴といった要素をももたらす。どのような風景がそこにあるのだろうか？どのようにそれを描写すればよいか？風景は何を意味しているのだろうか？
本セミナーにおいて、学生各自は、自ら選択し、注意深く鑑賞して分析・研究した映画を紹介する。学生は自由に映画を選択できる。紹介する映画は製作年代を問わず、日本映画、米国映画、その他の国の映画など、国籍も問わない。映画分析は、「好き・好きではない」「良い・良くない」といった個人的な意見を超越したものである。好きでない映画であっても、大変面白い分析をすることが可能である。

teacher: マルティ・オロバル　ベルナット
summary_excerpt: このゼミでは思想史学・宗教社会学という視座より、西洋・日本における宗教史に......
subtitle:
近世・近代における宗教思想
History of Religious Thought in Modern and Contemporary Times
summary:
このゼミでは思想史学・宗教社会学という視座より、西洋・日本における宗教史に対する理解を深め、宗教と社会、宗教と政治、宗教と道徳との関係について考えていきたい。「近代化と宗教」という問題、つまり近代化がもたらした様々な変化が宗教にどのような影響を与えたかを分析・理解するのがゼミの最終目標となる。先ず、近代は信教の自由と共に世俗化が進んだ時代であるといえる。その中で、科学の進歩と共に、新たな思想伝統が誕生し、宗教の意義を否定する思潮が台頭した。中には、近代化に適応し、宗教と科学を融合させようとした、宗教の内面化（最近の用語を使用すれば「マインドフルネス化」）を試みようとした宗教家も存在する。しかし、その一方で、宗教界において近代化・新たな思潮に反発した原理主義も誕生し、宗教アイデンティティ問題、宗教と国家主義との深い関係も見られる。この二つの要素、「近代」及び「宗教」の複雑な関係についてゼミ生と一緒に考えていきたい。
This seminar is dedicated to the study of the history of religion in the West and Japan from the perspective of the history of ideas and the sociology of religion. We will consider topics as the relationship between religion and society, religion and politics, and religion and morality. The final goal of the seminar is to analyze and understand the interrelation of modernization and religion, that is, how the changes produced by modernization have affected religion. It can be said that modernity, especially in the West, is an era when secularization has spread, along with religious freedom. Together with the progress of science, new traditions of thought were born, and new currents of thought denying the significance of religion emerged. Some religious thinkers have tried to adapt to modernization and combine religion and science, or to interiorize (privatize)religion (as it can be seen in recent phenomena as the “mindfulness” trend). On the other hand, a completely different reaction to modernity in the religious world is fundamentalism, which denies modernization and all the new currents of thought. This ideological retreat, which is fundamentalism, is also intimately related to other questions, as religious identity problems and the relation between religion and nationalism. In sum, I would like to reflect upon the complex relationship between "modernity" and "religion" together with the seminar students.
goal: ゼミの主な目的を以下の要点にまとめる
study_outside:
教科書は特になく、事前に、文献リスト、課題となる論文等を配布する。基本的には日本語で著された文献（学生の能力・ニーズに応じて外国語で書かれた著作も使用する）を読解、分析し、その内容について皆で自由に討論する。また、卒論を書きたい学生は自分自身で問いを立て、自分にとって最も面白い研究主題を絞り、卒業論文を完成させる。宗教に関するものであれば、研究テーマの選択は完全に自由である。卒業論文の執筆で使用する可能な言語は日本語、スペイン語、英語、フランス語またはカタルーニャ語である。
We will not use any textbooks. I will distribute the reading materials (academic papers or book chapters) in advance. Students must read and analyze documents in Japanese (also use works written in foreign languages depending on students' abilities and needs) and discuss the contents freely with everyone. However, if members of the EDP join the seminar, I will try to provide materials in English. Students who want to write a graduation thesis must find which topics are most interesting to them, narrow down their research topic, and complete their graduation thesis. As far as the research topic is related to religion, students have complete freedom to choose. Possible languages for writing the thesis are Japanese, English, Spanish, French, or Catalan.

summary:
私たちは現代社会のあらゆる場面で、話しことばの音声を聞いたり発したりして生活しています。
たとえば、授業中の先生の話、講演会、友人や家族との様々な場所・場面での会話、電話やオンラインツールを用いた会話、駅や電車のアナウンス、店員との会話、政治家のスピーチや討論、選挙演説、ニュース音声、オリンピックなどのスポーツ解説、スポーツ選手のコメント、テレビ番組や映画での会話、漫才の対話、アニメの声、詩の朗読、様々な方言、外国語の音声など。また、話しことばに近いものとしては、ＳＮＳでのチャットやスタンプ、絵文字などがあります。
話しことばの音声は、言語的な情報を伝達するだけでなく、話し手の感情やニュアンスや発話意図なども伝達します。
話しことばの音声は、皆さんの専門分野である政治学や経済学をはじめ、様々な学問領域とも密接に結びついています。
この演習では、以上挙げたような現代社会における話しことばに着目した研究を行います。

name: Intermediate Seminar (Introduction to Empirical Economics)　０１
summary_excerpt: The seminar is designed to guide you to an advanced study of modern empiri......
subtitle: Guidance to Empirical Economics
summary: The seminar is designed to guide you to an advanced study of modern empirical economics (e.g. labor, health, education, environment and urban economics). The seminar consists of two pillars. In the first pillar, we understand the importance of identifying the causality in contrast to correlation, and study popular methods of identification. In the second pillar, we read well-written academic papers, which are digestible for undergrads. The seminar proceeds with lectures and student presentations.
goal:
1. Learn the concepts of commonly used identification methods for empirical economics.
2. Become a good consumer of an academic empirical paper. Present it in an engaging way.
3. Craft a research proposal as input to your bachelor's thesis.
study_outside: Introductory microeconomics is required. Familiarity with econometrics or causal inference is an advantage.
schedule_plan:
1:
Introduction
I start by explain on the concepts of causal inference, essential for understanding modern empirical research.
2:
Academic Presentation
I show how to present an academic talk for your incoming presentations. I share good slides of previous students.
3:
Biases for Causal inference
I explain why it is detrimental to confuse with spurious correlation. We overview a list of pitfalls of systematic biases for inference; coincidence, omitted variables, compounding variables, selection and reverse causality. (e.g. the effect of distributing PCs to children?) Do some exercises to master the concepts.
4:
Research Design
We discuss how to construct a causal story and build a best design for empirical research.
5:
Academic paper 1 (student's talk)
"Where Have All the Workers Gone? An Inquiry into the Decline of the U.S. Labor Force Participation Rate", Alan Krueger (2017)
6:
Natural experiment
The best strategy to test a causality is running a experiment, which have been imported from natural science. Randomized controlled experiment (RCT) is supposed to be a king of identification, but it is practically costly to run RCTs. In that case, researchers search for experiments in the real world. We discuss this methodology compared to RCTs.
7:
Academic paper 2 (student's talk)
TBA
8:
Difference-in-Difference (DID) method
Running DID on the panel data is a basic causal inference technique. I elaborate the core idea of DID in contrast to a naive before-after analysis.
(e.g. the effect of speed delimit of highways on fatalities; minimum wage impact on employment)
9:
Academic paper 3 (student's talk)
TBA
10:
Instrumental variable (IV) method
Finding a good instrument for address the endogeneity is a very popular method. I explain the idea and assumptions of IV methods.
(e.g. a ratio of female managers and corporate value; does conscription reduce post-war wages?)
11:
Academic paper 4 (student's talk)
TBA
12:
Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
RDD is a quasi-experiment using discontinuous borders of a policy or institution of interest.  We discuss the conditions of RDD by showing some examples.
13:
Academic paper 5 (student's talk)
TBA
14:
Concluding lecture
I discuss limits of experimental approach, and introduce alternative structural approach. I also share the current trends in economics and provide career orientation to broadly-defined economist career after Master's or PhD.

summary_excerpt: Globalization is a highly contested term; there are many different and com......
subtitle: Economics and Politics of Globalization
summary: Globalization is a highly contested term; there are many different and competing understandings of what this concept means and how to assess the processes it entails. At the very basic, globalization refers to massive intensification of economic, political, social, and cultural relations across international borders. Such a simplistic definition however, is far from doing justice to a term which occupies an increasingly prominent place in today’s world. So this class aims to explore globalization studies further with a particular focus on political economy. We will not only discuss globalization from different theoretical perspectives but also analyze and critically think about various effects and challenges a rapidly integrating world causes on trade, finance, economic development as well as the institution of nation-states.
goal: At the end of the term, students will be able to grasp the factors which have led to the complex globalization processes and critically assess and evaluate the causes and effects of globalization on economic and political spheres.
study_outside: The class aims to connect lectures with active class discussions. The lectures will provide you with the basic theoretical perspectives and their practical applications. In the discussion sessions, we will engage in lively class debates around the topic of that week. In order to become an active participant in class discussions, students are required to complete all the assigned reading before coming to class.

name: Intermediate Seminar (Theoretical Psychology)　０１
summary_excerpt: According to the common understanding, theoretical psychology is the study......
subtitle: the Border between Perception and Cognition
summary:
According to the common understanding, theoretical psychology is the study of the philosophical, metapsychological, and foundational aspects of psychology. It has been officially recognised as part of the discipline of psychology form 1960s. However, this general description only brings up more questions: what is philosophy in this context? What is metapsychology anyway? How do we distinguish between fundamental and non-fundamental aspects of psychology? In this course, we will selectively introduce one specific area within theoretical psychology, and along the way strengthen our abilities of textual analysis and critical thinking.
The following weekly topics and readings are only tentative and subject to change. They will be modified according to the instructor’s and students’ academic interests. For now, we will be focussing on the theoretical border between perception and cognition.
goal: This course is under the heading of “Intermediate Seminar,” the main purpose of which is to focus on critical thinking through reading and writing analytically. Therefore, although we will seek to learn about the border issue within theoretical psychology, the bottom line is to learn about reading and understanding essays to begin with, and then trying to write in ways that can contribute to the literature. This implies that in most weeks we will not finish discussing the assigned readings, and in some weeks, we will continue the readings from the previous weeks, etc. The materials are food for thought, so we shall focus on the process of learning, without worrying too much about whether we finish the materials.

Overview
The first iteration of this course will be an exploration of a few basic areas of EFL practice and the conditions and policies in Japan. It is designed for non-expert participants who are not necessarily hoping to become specialists in any of the fields related to the topics we will discuss.
We will examine the basics of language teaching, starting with a few publications from the Council of Europe. Then we will turn our attention to a consideration of some current and future challenges for pedagogy and policy, including technological tools like generative artificial intelligence and sociopolitical implications of EFL as a required course in schools. Preparation
Most weeks, but not all, will have some required reading assigned, but usually no more than one academic article or chapter. These readings will be in English or Japanese. Students should be prepared to produce an unassisted spoken or pencil-and-paper written response.

In the second half of the semester, students will work on an individual or group project on a topic of interest that will culminate in a presentation with oral Q&A.
There will also be an in-class pencil-and-paper essay test at one point during the course and one at the end. These will cover content from the readings and class discussions.
All of my communications, including lectures, course management materials and assignment feedback, will be in English. However, students are welcome to speak in class and submit work in either English or Japanese. I will make grammar and word-choice corrections for essay test submissions in that are in English. summary:
This module aims to provide a resolutely unorthodox introduction to contemporary moral and political philosophy.
Taking a cue from Rebecca Buxton and Lisa Whiting’s 2020 book
The Philosopher Queens
, it re-imagines the development of contemporary moral and political philosophy by focusing exclusively on women’s contributions. What does the discipline look like if we replace ‘men of ideas’ – John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Jürgen Habermas and so on – with their female counterparts, such as Simone de Beauvoir, Iris Murdoch, Hannah Arendt, and Judith Shklar? Discussion topics include some of the major issues in moral and political philosophy such as power, freedom and liberalism. But we will also explore a set of issues many philosophers today are afraid of addressing: the relationship between philosophy and literature.

name: Intermediate Seminar (Consequentialism: Critical Perspectives)　０１
summary_excerpt: Consequentialism is the view that it is always correct to choose actions o......
summary:
Consequentialism is the view that it is always correct to choose actions or policies that promote the best outcomes. It may seem obvious that actions and policies are justified wholly by the good consequences they bring about. Yet, this deceptively simple idea is also one of the most hotly disputed in contemporary political philosophy. For instance: How do we define what the "best" outcome is? Is it the outcome that leads to the most happiness overall, or do other non-welfaristic values matter as well? Are consequences the only thing that matters for the evaluation of the rightness of actions, or does it matter how those consequences are brought about, for example, without violating the rights of others? (In other words, do "the ends always justify the means"?) In this course, students will gain a nuanced understanding of these issues through critically engaging with some of the foundational texts in the contemporary literature on consequentialism.
This is a seminar-style course, with an emphasis on in-class discussion and careful engagement with the assigned readings. Each week, students are expected to complete the readings beforehand and to bring their questions and comments to class.
goal: 1. To gain an understanding of the key features of consequentialism and its significance for political thought.

Equality is a contested political value. Many people believe that unequal institutions and policies are, to that extent, unjust. summary_excerpt: Japan currently faces various diplomatic challenges: friction with neighbo......
summary:
Japan currently faces various diplomatic challenges: friction with neighbouring Northeast Asian countries over
historical problems or territorial issues; fragile relations with South Korea and continuing tensions with North Korea over the abductees and nuclear weapons.  Furthermore, as China grows ever stronger, the East Asian security environment has been transformed, and tensions across the Taiwan Strait have risen. Elsewhere, in the aftermath of Hamas’s attack on Israel, Gaza has been devastated and confrontation between Iran and the USA has included military action, and looks poised to become a general war.  In Europe, there is still no easy path to the end of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.  At home, there is sporadic debate over whether and how Japan should expand its military role in responding to such threats, both regional and global, in the form of revision of the constitution.  In addition, there is still strong opposition in Okinawa to the building of a new base in preparation for the proposed closure of the Futenma Air Base.  Further, the COVID-19 pandemic made everyone more aware of the need for international responses to global issues, whether future pandemics or environmental issues. Given this situation, how should international peace and stability be established?  What international commitments should Japan undertake, and what are the domestic conditions for such commitments?
As an important first step towards answering this question, this course provides an introductory survey of post-war Japanese international relations, with particular emphasis on the development of the US-Japan alliance and the evolution of relations between Japan and neighbouring Asian states. Through the analysis and explanation of historical events, particular efforts will be made to place those events that relate to Japan in the context of transformations in the structure of wider international relations. Special attention will also be paid to the alternative approaches that may have been available to the Japanese government, and their likely outcomes.  The course thereby aims to provide both an historical grounding and the analytical perspectives necessary to understand the significant changes currently developing in Japan’s political and international milieu.
Most of the course will be made up of weekly lectures.
However, in order to help deepen understanding of the issues, each class will also include a short class discussion.

summary:
In the most basic sense, writing is the ability to fully and accurately express your thoughts, whether to another human reader or as a command to a machine. Fortunately students in the SPSE are all very well-educated, with a rich set of educational, professional and personal experiences, so your ideas are very complex and insightful. Crucially, however, ideas like these require a very high level of expressive ability, and even if you have this in your native language, reaching that level in English, your second (or third or fourth) language, will take a bit of work and insightfulness. Verbal and written expression is a core human ability, so every human being, especially those with rich backgrounds like you, can learn to do it well, if they choose to spend the time and make the effort.
The advanced level of this writing series is for learners who are at CEFR level B2+ or C1, which implies that you can write a reasonable paragraph without making a mistake every sentence, using just a pen and paper and no other resources.
In order to be considered for enrollment in this course please sign up for the on-campus, pen-and-paper placement test by January 8, 2026 at 17:00 JST.
If you are a current student, please be sure to include your ID number with your name when you sign up. If you are a new student, include your examination number with your name.  Test sign-up link: https://forms.office.com/r/mfUFUJU23N
The test will be administered on Saturday January 24, 2026 at 13:10 and Monday January 26, 2026 at 17:00 in Building 3 Room YYY. Please bring a pen or pencil and your student ID or some other sort of photo identification.
In this course, we will work on improving use of complex grammar, expanding vocabulary and developing structured arguments, focusing mostly at the paragraph and essay level. These goals will be accomplished by analyzing specific news, business and academic texts and then composing texts both with and without online tools. Students will get detailed feedback and / or corrections on at least 7 major assignments. There will be in-class writing during each meeting, either on paper or online (or both), so students should bring both a laptop or similar device as well as a pen or pencil every day. Writing assignments will also include homework essays that allow the use of online tools. Note that the course schedule listed is tentative and may change substantially depending on the specific needs of enrolled students.
goal:
If you think good writing is about getting the right answer or getting a good grade, this course is not for you. However, if you want to be able to learn how to effectively communicate your ideas in writing, then this course is for you.
We will focus on writing that is analytical and above all reflective. Topics include approaches to vocabulary and syntax as well as a discussion of logic and rhetoric. We will also address writing about data, and dealing with complications, using hedging and qualification. There will also be some emphasis on writing for different audiences.
It goes without saying that we are in a transition period, where the meaning of "writing" in educational settings is changing. As such, this course does not cover the topic of research papers. It can be argued that, to a very large extent, that format is no longer useful in undergraduate writing courses. It is more appropriate in specific research or creative situations where the writer is contributing something new, which would be, by definition, something that generative artificial intelligence cannot do.
This course will help you understand your own writing proficiency level and identify specific steps to improve it. You will learn to identify the differences in vocabulary, grammar and structure that distinguish higher level writing proficiency in academic, business and other writing.

For weekly preparation, students are expected to read all posted material and come to class ready to take a quiz, write a response and / or discuss the material with or without access to the text or the internet. Weekly preparation time should be no longer than 100 minutes. Homework will not be assigned every week, but when it is, it should take no more than 100 minutes for each assignment.

This course will involve two take-home assignments that will be graded and then critiqued in class.

Three things won’t be tolerated in this class.
The first is using work without attribution, making up quotes, inventing “facts” and cutting and pasting text from other sources – and passing them off as your own. These actions can not only land you in legal problems, they hurt the entire profession of journalism. They constitute severe ethics violations. If I notice such slip ups in your work, I will automatically give that assignment a Zero, and I will address the matter to the faculty of the journalism school.
The second sin is missing an assignment deadline. You are not allowed to miss a deadline on the job, and you won’t be allowed to in class either. In most cases, it is better to turn in something incomplete or imperfect than to miss a deadline. Points will be deducted for late work.
The final issue is unprofessionalism. Journalism is about the free-flow and exchange of information. It is imperative that you speak up in class and respect the rights of others to speak as well. A large part of the class will involve critiquing the work you hand in. We must not only accept criticism gracefully and with good humor but also offer it in a constructive way. The critiques are meant to help each of us improve. They are not supposed to be a stage for put downs.

I was with the AP for eight years, with postings in Portland, Oregon; New York City; Frankfurt, Germany; Tokyo and Seoul, South Korea. I have also worked as an editor for Bloomberg News and as a reporter for Voice of America Radio, in Hong Kong and New York. I am currently the Tokyo-based Asia Editor for

I have netted numerous U.S. business journalism prizes for my reporting on Toyota, Hyundai, Japan’s 2011 earthquake-tsunami disaster, the Chinese auto industry and price fixing. I was born near Detroit, Michigan, in the United States. I have a bachelor’s degree in political science and philosophy from the University of Michigan and a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University.
HELP:
People don’t become good journalists all by themselves. Throughout my career, I owe immeasurable thanks to dozens of editors, bosses, colleagues and teachers who took the time to help me become better. I strongly encourage you to approach me whenever you are having problems in the class. I also urge you not to be shy in asking questions, in class and after class. One secret to being a good journalist is never being afraid to ask a question, even if you think it may be “stupid.”

subtitle: Oscar Wilde, Bernard Shaw, and the 1890s
summary:
This course is intended primarily for students who may be familiar with the names of Oscar Wilde and George Bernard Shaw but have never read any of their works from start to finish. We will read a play each by those two authors:
Lady Windermere's Fan
and
Mrs. Warren's Profession
. Wilde's play, which premiered in 1892, achieved a commercial success on the London stage, while Shaw's play, written only a year later, was initially banned from performance. Throughout the course, we will analyze and discuss the two plays in the context of late-nineteenth-century English society.
The course will first take up
Lady Windermere's Fan
, which has a young, upper-class woman as the protagonist. We will then read
Mrs. Warren's Profession
, a play whose narrative also features a young woman but in a very different setting. We will talk about how Shaw's play is a social commentary on Wilde's play. Our primary themes will be women, family values, morality, class, equality/inequality in Victorian England. It is hoped that students will look beyond Victorian England and test their analyses of the plays against other social circumstances at other points in time.

name: Introduction to Political Analysis　０１
summary_excerpt: This course is designed as an overview of empirical political science and ......
summary:
This course is designed as an overview of empirical political science and as an introduction to important concepts, theories, methods, and findings in the discipline. While it is impossible to survey completely the broad field of political science, the course will acquaint students with some of the major questions in political science and encourage students to think critically about the discipline’s best answers to those questions.
This course will cover basic concepts relevant to the study of different types of political systems (such as democracy or sovereignty). Students will become familiar with the challenges of defining and measuring such concepts (for example, how much more democratic is Japan than China?) and will also acquire some historical understanding of these concepts (how did the sovereign state system come about?). Students will learn how scholars understand political behavior (both peaceful and violent), political culture, and political identity (of various forms, including class, ethnicity, religion and gender). Students will also be exposed to the study of political institutions (analyzing, in particular, how different constitutional rules either concentrate or disperse political power). Finally, this course will examine how political scientists assess causal relationships between social, economic and political variables (for example, does economic development promote democratization?).
goal: * Students will learn concepts and methods of analysis used in the contemporary discipline of political science.
study_outside:
As a 4 credit course, this class meets twice a week. The first session will be conducted in lecture format. Although attendance does not explicitly factor into the course grade, students must attend lectures and take notes in order to do well on the exam because the lecture material differs substantially from the textbook.
The second session will be conducted as a workshop in smaller classes, each led by a TA. The workshops will involve small group activities and discussion to foster active learning. Each week there will be a short assignment that reinforces the class material. Attendance and active participation are important.
The in-class, handwritten final exam will consist of analytical problems and/or broad questions that typically require multi-paragraph answers.

summary_excerpt: The main goal of this course is to provide an overview of modern Japanese ......
summary:
The main goal of this course is to provide an overview of modern Japanese political history. Since the late 19th century, Japan has been undoubtedly one of the most influential countries in Asia. Exploration of Japan’s efforts to deal with various domestic and foreign issues during this period will allow us to better understand Asia’s past and present as well as those of Japan.
Modern Japanese history has witnessed fluctuations between democratization and militarization, as well as between unilateralism and multilateralism. To comprehend the process of oscillation clearly, this course will also analyze the dynamic interplay between domestic politics and diplomacy. By doing so, it aims to enhance participants' ability to think critically about modern Japanese history.
We first focus on nation state building, demise of the status system internally and restoration of sovereignty externally. Based on the subsequent early development of political parties, we will illustrate how the promulgation of the Imperial Constitution and the inauguration of the Imperial Diet changed the political landscape. We will move on to the rise and fall of party politics in addition to Japan’s pursuit of "Empire" and its political impacts until the end of World War II. Lastly, the course will also examine political and diplomatic developments in the postwar era, highlighting the complicated legacy of World War II, while also considering transwar continuities.

summary_excerpt: This course examines global economic history from 1500 to 1900 through a “......
subtitle: Decentered Global Economic History (1500-1900)
summary: This course examines global economic history from 1500 to 1900 through a “polycentric” and “connected histories” framework, moving beyond traditional Eurocentric narratives. Rather than portraying Europe as the sole driver of economic change, the course highlights the role of Asian, African, and American actors in shaping the global economic order. The course is organised in four parts: (1) the polycentric world before European expansion, (2) early connections that modified but did not destroy existing systems, (3) the multiple paths of the Great Divergence, and (4) the consolidation of an unequal world system. Throughout, it will also integrate environmental and gender perspectives as essential analytical lenses. Key topics include Asian maritime trading systems, global silver flows, plantation economies, the industrious revolution, the Great Divergence debate, and systems of coerced and contractual labour.

name: Advanced Topics in Economics: Global History of Money and Finance　０１
teacher: オーレグレン　アンダシュ／鎮目　雅人
summary_excerpt: This course analyses and discusses the concepts of money and finance, draw......
summary:
This course analyses and discusses the concepts of money and finance, drawing on both theory and empirical evidence. The main question is the apparent contradiction that financial systems are important for economic development yet are also prone to instability (crises). This course discusses the concept of money both historically and present, and different international monetary systems. We explore why monetary systems change, the pros and cons of fixed exchange rates, currency unions, currency boards and floating exchange rates, and how monetary systems relate to political and economic factors. The linkages between the fiscal and the monetary systems, sovereign and foreign debt. We also discuss the pros and cons of central and free banking, the effects of different kinds of monetary policy interventions. We examine financial crises, their causes and remedies, and why some financial institutions fail during crises while others do not. Finally, we will also examine cryptoassets/currencies and central bank digital currencies. Throughout, we contrast theory with historical empirics.

goal: After this course students should have a profound understanding of monetary theories and monetary systems. Understand the interlinkages between money and finance, financial crises, the role of central banks, crisis management and the effects of monetary policies. The student should also have knowledge of different kinds of cryptoassets/currencies and their challenges.
study_outside: Students should read the required readings before the class and take part in the discussion. Some of the articles are quite technical, but the mathematical derivation is not important. What is important are the assumptions made and the conclusions drawn.

Session 1: Money in economic theory and practice. The Mundell trilemma and international monetary regimes. Q&A
This session discusses money in theory and practice, and how our theoretical ideas about money do not always match practice. It introduces the ideas surrounding money, how we define money, and how 'monetary value' is created in an economy.

This is a general site for the history of economic thought where you can find a lot of material and original historical writings on monetary issues.

2:
October 14 Money in theory and practice 2
Session 2: The power to issue money: Free banking, central banking, Modern monetary theory, Bitcoin. Q&A
This session, which is a continuation of our first session, focuses on debunking some of the myths surrounding money. By looking at how money is created and by whom, we discuss the extent to which the way money is created today shapes the shape of our economies and social fabric. Who should have the power to issue money? And for what purpose? What is the theoretical and empirical evidence on money creation? And how should we understand the technology and function of bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies in this context?

3:
October 21 Money in theory and practice 3
Session 3: Sovereign money, Central banks and central bank digital currencies. Q&A
While the Free Banking School argues against central banks and any kind of government-issued money, a number of economists and political movements are arguing for governments and central banks to take back the power to issue most of our money. From the Positive Money movement to Modern Monetary Theorists, sovereign money is being put back on the agenda. At the same time, central banks and central bankers are faced with a growing number of alternative currencies challenging their mandate to issue money. In an attempt to adapt to this situation, central banks are putting more and more resources into the development of so-called Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs). However, the idea that the government (political authority) should control the issuance of money is not new and has been tried throughout history with varying degrees of success. What are the differences between sovereign monetary systems in history and today? Does new technology solve these problems? What problems remain? Do these potential solutions create other problems? If so, which ones?

Session 4: Old problems, new technologies: South Sea and Mississippi bubbles vs OneCoin, FTX, Terra/Luna etc Q&A
A widely debated question regarding cryptocurrencies is whether they should be considered money or financial instruments/assets. In this session we will explore the similarities and differences behind some of the most famous financial and monetary events in history, the Mississippi and South Sea bubbles in the early 18th century, with various cryptocurrency bubbles such as BitConnect, OneCoin, TerraLuna and FTX. We'll study the introduction of the stable-coin Tether and its link to the USD, as well as other cryptocurrencies and exchanges such as Bitcoin, FTX, Alameda Research and Binance. Through these cases we analyse the relationship between money and debt, both sovereign and private, and how the power to issue money/debt affects the rules of the game for all who come into contact with this 'money' in any way. To do so we introduce the famous ‘Minsky-Kindleberger Crisis Anatomy’ and discuss its validity for analyzing financial crises.

summary_excerpt: This course is a tour d’horizon of the study of international relations de......
summary:
This course is a tour d’horizon of the study of international relations dealing with the problem of war
and peace and the models of global governance
.  Global governance is the buzzword de jour that is
at
the center of gravity in the scholarship of social science.  It is meant to encompass more than classical descriptions of system structure (hegemonic, bipolar), more than the field of international organization, and to include current concerns about the ways in which order will be maintained in various areas of world politics.  The phrase captures the sense that there is governance at the global stage even though it differs from domestic governments.  The modern history of international politics has evolved around the innovations in governing principles for the world order and the strategies for global governance.  The core question of global governance remains that of peace and war.
This course
will survey key topics and issues in the study of world politics, ranging from the nature of the international system, the cause and consequence of international conflict to the difficulty of international cooperation.  Specific topics include the causes of war and conditions for peace, domestic incentives for war, alliance and collective security, civil wars and terrorism, the politics of nuclear weapons, the role of international organizations, the structure of international system(s), power transition theory to name a few.  We will also explore the politics of international trade, monetary relations, and financial relations as times allows. When appropriate, we will reference the contemporary and current international affairs as the motivation and illustrations of some of these topics. Since the School of Political Science and Economics also offers courses on International/Global Political Economy, this course will not spend much time on the politics of international finance, currency, or trade.  Similarly, PSE offers a variety of courses on democracy, this course will not deal with those issues.
goal:
• To be able to think critically and analytically about contemporary international affairs.
• To be able to use evidence to evaluate arguments and discourse on international politics.
• To obtain basic theoretical and conceptual tools to understand international politics.
• To prepare for more advanced courses in international relations.

• Puzzle of War essay: You will answer the questions related to the theories on the causes of war, based on the lectures. The essay is expected to be two to three-page long, double-spaced. The essay is at least three-page long, double-spaced but should not exceed five pages. We adopt a peer-review system. name: Political Communication　０１
summary_excerpt: This course is an introduction to political communication. After an overvi......
summary: This course is an introduction to political communication. After an overview of the history of media effects theories, the lecture will address the major issues of political communication in contemporary politics. The lecture will not only introduce students to U.S.-based political communication research, but also develop an academic perspective on real-life political communication by connecting it to current issues in East Asia. In addition, students will practice using the theories and models introduced in the lectures to analyze political phenomena.
goal: The goal is for students to be able to examine the relationship between politics, media, and public opinion from academic perspectives. In particular, students should be able to gain an overview of media effects research and use major theories and models to understand contemporary political communication phenomena.
study_outside: To be announced in the class.
schedule_plan:
1:
Week 1: Introduction
The lecture will outline political communication research as the intersection between politics, media, and public opinion.
2:
Week 2: Media effects theories
The transition from powerful effects theory to limited effects theory will be described to introduce early media effects theories.
3:
Week 3: Cognitive revolution
The cognitive effects of the media will be outlined with a focus on agenda-setting, priming, and framing.
4:
Week 4: Indirect effects theories
The indirect effects of the media on public opinion will be outlined, focusing on the third-person effect and the spiral of silence.
5:
Week 5: Emergence of new media
How media effects theories have been modified from the advent of cable television and the internet to the proliferation of social media will be outlined, focusing on the new powerful effects theory and the minimal effects theory.
6:
Week 6: Social media
Focusing on social media, the lecture will outline the relationship between selective exposure and political polarization.
7:
Week 7: Media and political learning
Focusing on the relationship between media use and the levels of political knowledge, the lecture will outline the knowledge gap hypothesis and the effects of incidental learning.
8:
Week 8: Media and collective action
The lecture will outline how social media is used as a tool for mobilization in large-scale protests. Particular attention will be paid to its role as a platform for spreading narratives and gaining collective intelligence.
9:
Week 9: Authoritarianism and the internet
The lecturer will outline how authoritarian states use the media to control domestic public opinion and to exercise international propaganda and sharp power.
10:
Week 10: Quality of news
The lecturer will provide an overview of the factors on the supply side of news. In particular, it will explain the impact of competition and regulation on the quality of news and the resulting rise of soft news.
11:
Week 11: The role of public broadcasting
The lecture will provide an overview of the role that public broadcasting plays in democracy. In particular, the lecture will address the issue of the relationship between NHK and Japanese politics.
12:
Week 12: Organizational factors in the media
The lecture will provide an overview of organizational factors in news production. In particular, the gatekeeping and indexing functions of the media will be introduced.
13:
Week 13: Media and international relations
The lecture will outline the relationship between media and international relations, particularly the evolution of war coverage and the in-group bias of international news.
14:
Week 14: Media system theory
With the media system theory, the lecture will outline the relationship between media, macro social structures, and historical backgrounds. In explaining the typology of media systems, the lecture will also explain the characteristics of the Japanese media system.
textbook: Iyengar, S. (2022). Media politics: A citizen's guide (Fifth Edition). W. W. Norton & Company.

summary_excerpt: This course teaches public finance at its introductory level. The topics r......
summary: This course teaches public finance at its introductory level. The topics range from normative issues, such as why and how we need the government to intervene in the market economy, to positive ones, such as how it intervenes in the economy in reality. A basic understanding of introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics is required.
goal: This course aims to provide students with a basic understanding of Japan’s public finance system and a basis for thinking about the desirable design of the system.
study_outside: A basic understanding of introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics is required.
schedule_plan:
1:
Class 1: Introduction
I overview the overview the origin and development of public finance. The course plan and grading policy will be explained.
2:
Class 2: Roles of governments
What roles should governments or public sectors play? I explain this from the viewpoint of the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.
3:
Class 3: Scope of governments and budget systems (1)
What do governments means differ depending on the context. I explain the governments and related organizations in the system of national accounts.
4:
Class 4: Scope of governments and budget systems (2)
How the government budgets are formulated in Japan? I explain the process and discuss the roles of FILP (financial investment and loan program).
5:
Class 5: Public investment and public capital
The public capital in Japan was said to be excessive. I overview the public investment in recent years and discuss how to evaluate the public investment plans and cost-benefit analysis.
6:
Class 6: Local public finance and intergovernmental relationship (1)
The local governments in Japan play a significant role in implementing government tasks. I explain the basics of the local public finance system in Japan.
7:
Class 7: Local public finance and intergovernmental relationship (2)
A design of local public finance system, especially intergovernmental transfers, is crucial when local governments play a significant role. I explain the basic theory and Japanese intergovernmental transfer system.
8:
Class 8: Tax systems and their effects (1)
Government expenditures are basically financed by tax revenues. I explain the taxation principles and tax structures in Japan.
9:
Class 9: Tax systems and their effects (2)
One of the major taxes in Japan is the personal income tax. I explain the basic system of the Japanese personal income tax system and the effects from the microeconomic viewpoint.
10:
Class 10: Public pension
A significant part of Japanese government expenditures is for the social security system. I explain the public old-age pension insurance system and its effects.
11:
Class 11: Public health insurances
The health care costs are increasing as a percentage of GDP. I explain the basics of Japanese health care system and health insurance system.
12:
Class 12: Budget balance
Japanese governments has a huge public debt. I explain the intertemporal budget constraint of government and how to decrease the debt-to-GDP ratio.
13:
Class 13: Ricardian equivalence
How should we consider the huge public debt? I explain the Ricardian equivalence theorem and its implications.
14:
Class 14: Review
A final exam will be given to evaluate your understanding of the overall content of the class

summary_excerpt: This is an intermediate course in game theory for undergraduate school stu......
summary:
This is an intermediate course in game theory for undergraduate school students.  Game theory is the mathematical analysis of strategic decision-making.  The bulk of the course is organized around classes of "games" (representations of strategic environments).  For each class of games, we will develop and learn to use one or more "solution concepts" (methods of deriving predictions).  Applications of game theory extend well beyond economics to political science, engineering, computer science, finance, biology, anthropology, sociology, and other fields.  We will analyze some of these applications in class.
The prerequisite for undergraduate students is Introduction to Game Theory (ゲーム理論入門). I also assume that students are familiar with basic differential calculus and basic probability theory. What is more important than any specific previous coursework is some degree of comfort with the material presented formally (i.e., mathematical).
goal: Students are expected to understand the equilibrium concepts in game theory and how to apply them. Students are also expected to be able to read academic papers and books related to applied game theory.

name: Japanese Political Thought B　０１
teacher: ミドルトン　ベンヤミン・デュガルド／梅森　直之
summary_excerpt: This course will examine the development and transformation of modern Japa......
subtitle: Fascism, War Memory and Hyper-Economic Development
summary:
This course will examine the development and transformation of modern Japanese political thought. Our focus will be from the Shōwa period (1926-89) to the Reiwa period (2019-today). Major themes are: the analysis of fascism by Japanese and Western political theorists; the lived experience of fascism in Japan and its colonies; the formation of postwar memory and amnesia; the politics of unresolved issues from the wartime period, such as the comfort women and Yasukuni Shrine issues; the politics of apology; postwar hyper-economic development and its externalities; and democracy. Using empirical and theoretical perspectives, we will study both the historical and contemporary significance of these topics.
The course will be taught in English, so no knowledge of Japanese is required.
A basic knowledge of modern Japanese history is helpful, but not required. If you need background information, please consult the works listed in the Reference Materials section below.
goal: 1. Acquiring knowledge of modern Japanese political thought.
study_outside: The reading load is about two essays or book chapters per session. Students are expected to do the readings in advance so that they can contribute to discussions in class. To facilitate deeper interaction, students will also participate in discussion forums on Waseda Moodle. Students are also required to give two presentations during the term: a mid-term presentation on hyperart; and a research presentation about their term paper (on a topic of their choice).
schedule_plan:
1:
Introduction
Welcome to the course!
2:
The Asia-Pacific War in History and Memory
We will gain an overview of the history of Asia-Pacific War and discuss some of its political implications.
3:
War Responsibility and War Guilt
We will examine the philosophy of guilt and discuss how political leaders have responded to calls for Japan to accept war responsibility and war guilt.
4:
Theorizing Japanese Fascism
We will engage with the work of leading Japanese and Western theorists of fascism and examine how people who lived through the fascist era in Japan worked through it after 1945.
5:
The Comfort Women Issue in Memory and Politics
We will discuss the legacy of the comfort woman issue and the responses of political leaders.
6:
The Comfort Women Issue: Fieldtrip
We will visit the a museum close to campus that focuses on the comfort women issue to gain insight into the scope and scale of the issue, and hear the voices of some of the victims. Details will be posted to the course Moodle site.
7:
The US Occupation of Japan and the IMTFE (Tokyo Trials)
How did the US Occupation and the Tokyo Trial create the baseline for Japanese memory work in the postwar era?
8:
Hyperart and Global 1968
We will discuss how the global youth counter-movements known as “Global 1968” manifested in Japan, using the artist Akasegawa Genpei as an example. This discussion will also examine how Japan’s political thought, which had centered on issues of fascism and war, transformed in the context of the new experience of hyper-development.
9:
War Memory and War Crimes
We will discuss Japanese and European theoretical approaches to collective memory and war memory, and use documentary films and texts to examine Japanese postwar responses to war crimes.
10:
Hyperart Field-Research Presentations
Students will present on their hyperart project in class.
11:
Industrial Pollution and Socio-Environmental Crisis: Minamata
We will examine Minamata Disease as a shadow history brought about by Japan’s hyper-economic development. Why and how did this tragic pollution-related disease occur? How did people perceive it, and how did they fight against it? To what extent was the anti-pollution movement as a continuation of the struggle against wartime elites and fascism?
12:
Mourning and Memorializing the Dead: Yasukuni Shrine
We will discuss the significance of the Yasukuni Shrine as a site of mourning and war memory, and the genealogy of the controversy that has rocked it in recent years.
13:
Yasukuni Shrine and Chidorigafuchi National Cemetery Field Trip
This week we will visit Yasukuni Shrine, the adjacent Yūshūkan museum, and nearby Chidorigafuchi National Cemetery to reflect on how war and the war dead are memorialized.
14:
Student Research Presentations
Students will present their final research project in class.

name: Advanced Seminar II　(Kellam, M)
summary_excerpt: Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains re......
subtitle: Comparative Politics of Developing Countries
summary:
Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains relationships between social, economic and political variables while focusing on politics within countries. Comparison is a defining feature of the subfield, and a key component in scientific study more generally. Thus, comparative politics uses cross-national comparisons (as well as comparisons of change over time) to understand why political systems are free or not free, stable or unstable, violent or peaceful, stagnant or productive, etc.
Comparative politics is a very broad field of inquiry; this seminar does not aim to be comprehensive but rather to delve deeply and critically into specific themes and countries that interest seminar participants. Building upon the basic knowledge of the developing world that we acquired in the previous seminar, in Advanced Seminar 2 students will read scholarly journal articles that they select on a topic that interests them. While the topics/countries will depend upon the particular interests of the seminar participants, we will keep our focus on the Global South (rather than the developed countries of Western Europe or Japan, for instance).
Looking ahead, the focus in Advanced Seminars 3 & 4 will turn to research design and methods in comparative politics, and to developing students’ projects in order to complete a thesis.
goal: * To increase the breadth and depth of students' knowledge of comparative politics
study_outside: Over the course of the semester, each participant will study a topic that interests them and share what they learn each week with the rest of the seminar participants. Every week all seminar participants will submit a short assignment on a Moodle forum before class and then discuss it during class. Most of these assignments should be about 200 words long, but occasionally they will be a bit longer or more involved.

The purpose of oral presentations is to share each student's work in the class, as well as for the instructor to test each student's understanding of the content of his/her essay.
In each class, a few students will be assigned to present the summary of the assigned textbook chapter.
All classes are held in person, unless otherwise announced at the course website on Waseda Moodle.

summary:
This seminar offers a brief introduction to the Economics of Information. The basic models of moral hazard, adverse selection and signaling will be analyzed to understand how markets function when market participants have asymmetric information. We will discuss how asymmetric information may lead to market breakdown and how appropriately designed contracts can help alleviate the adverse effect of asymmetric information on market efficiency.
This course requires the knowledge of basic economic concepts and microeconomic models. It is structured in a seminar format, therefore there will be no formal lectures.
This is a “no-essay seminar”. Students will be required to answer directed questions and solve numerous exercises during the course and in the final take-home exam (problem set).
goal: The aim of the course is to solve simple economic models with asymmetric information using game-theoretic tools in order to offer a concise introduction to the academic literature related to the topic. A variety of applications (e.g., labor contracts, price discrimination, insurance markets, marketing) will be discussed along with empirical findings from the experimental laboratory.
study_outside: Students are expected to read the assigned material before coming to class. Students will be required to work on assignments and make presentations in class individually or in groups.

subtitle: Comparative Politics of Developing Countries
summary:
Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains relationships between social, economic and political variables while focusing on politics within countries. Comparison is a defining feature of the subfield, and a key component in scientific study more generally. Thus, comparative politics uses cross-national comparisons (as well as comparisons of change over time) to understand why political systems are free or not free, stable or unstable, violent or peaceful, stagnant or productive, etc.
Comparative politics is a very broad field of inquiry; this seminar does not aim to be comprehensive but rather to delve deeply and critically into specific themes and countries that interest seminar participants. Building upon the basic knowledge of the developing world that we acquired in the previous seminar, in Advanced Seminar 2 students will read scholarly journal articles that they select on a topic that interests them. While the topics/countries will depend upon the particular interests of the seminar participants, we will keep our focus on the Global South (rather than the developed countries of Western Europe or Japan, for instance).
Looking ahead, the focus in Advanced Seminars 3 & 4 will turn to research design and methods in comparative politics, and to developing students’ projects in order to complete a thesis.
goal: * To increase the breadth and depth of students' knowledge of comparative politics
study_outside: Over the course of the semester, each participant will study a topic that interests them and share what they learn each week with the rest of the seminar participants. Every week all seminar participants will submit a short assignment on a Moodle forum before class and then discuss it during class. Most of these assignments should be about 200 words long, but occasionally they will be a bit longer or more involved.

subtitle: Social Data Science / Political Methodology
summary:
Social data science is an emerging academic field where researchers use statistics and programming to analyze or change society. Key is to understand human beings and their interactions behind data.
Political methodology is a subfield of political science focused on the development of quantitative tools for empirical political analysis. A relative of econometrics, psychometrics, biostatistics, etc., it is the "stats division" of political science.
If you liked Statistics I/II and want to learn more techniques for scientifically analyzing politics, policies, and society, this seminar will be a good fit for you.
This course is the first part of the four-semester seminar sequence designed to train you as a social data scientist / political methodologist. Being trained as a political methodologist will make you a perfect candidate for a data scientist at a tech company, as well as a graduate program in political science focused on quantitative analysis (either at Waseda or abroad).
The second semester of the sequence will be continuation of the first semester, which is a "boot camp" on statistics and data science research skills. The class will cover various quantitative techniques and their theoretical background frequently used in quantitative political science. The class will consist of a mixture of lectures, discussions, lab exercises, and presentations. Grades will be based on participation and weekly/term-end deliverables (there will be no exam).
goal: The goal of the first-year seminar is for you to acquire all the statistics and programming basics required for starting your own research project in the second year of the sequence. In other words, this seminar will allow you to:
study_outside:
Each week, background reading and/or materials will be provided so students will come to the class prepared for the lecture, discussion, or lab exercises. Students should expect to spend 1-2 hours on those.
In some weeks, there will be assignments to be completed after the class. They are typically programming exercises started during the week's lab session. Required hours will vary, but expect to spend up to 1-2 hours.

name: International Political Economy　０１
summary_excerpt: How does liberalization in international trade, finance, or migration chan......
summary:
How does liberalization in international trade, finance, or migration change the political power structure both within and across countries? Does globalization undermine democracy or strengthen it? If freer trade can generate mutual gains, why do governments still adopt protectionist policies? Do certain domestic political institutions help countries attract more foreign direct investments? How can states cooperate to prevent or manage global financial crises? What are the political intentions behind foreign aid? What makes people opposed to open immigration policies? Do multinational firms now wield political influence comparable to that of some states? Do expanding global value chains help spread human rights norms, or do they impede them? How can countries coordinate on climate change when they also prioritize economic growth?
These are some questions that studies of International Political Economy (IPE) have addressed. IPE examines how cross-border economic activity is shaped by domestic politics, interstate politics, and international institutions. It also investigates how global economic integration, in turn, impacts domestic and international politics. This course introduces major questions in the field and discuss various viewpoints across core issue areas, including trade, foreign investment, monetary and financial policy, development, the environment, globalization, and international institutions.
Classes will be held primarily in person. Some weeks may be covered by on-demand online sessions. Approximately 15 minutes of each class will be allocated to class discussion. The discussion format may be subject to change depending on the class size.

name: Theories in Comparative Politics　０１
teacher: ベナサリオ　ベルルッキ　アントニオ
summary_excerpt: Comparative politics is a field of political science that examines the dom......
summary:
Comparative politics is a field of political science that examines the domestic politics of different countries, or variation over time in political outcomes within a single country. It is called "comparative" because scholars in this area rely on cross-national and within-country comparisons to explain why certain political phenomena occur in some contexts, but not in others.
The course introduces leading theories and analytical frameworks in comparative politics, with a focus on political systems, institutions, and behaviors. Throughout the semester, we will address important questions such as "Does democracy require economic development?", "Are authoritarian regimes more efficient than democracies?", and "What is populism, why is it on the rise, and how does it affect politics today?"
goal: The course offers a systematic review of major theories in comparative politics. This gives students the opportunity to engage critically with the topics and build the foundations needed to explore research questions of their own interest. By the end of the course, they will be able to analyze politics using evidence-based approaches and will have developed the skills to make informed and original interpretations. In-class activities such as group work and discussions are an essential part of the course, and students are expected to participate actively.
study_outside: Academic articles or book chapters will be uploaded on Moodle each week. Students are expected to read them before coming to class. Occasionally, short written assignments will be given to assess their understanding of the readings and to encourage critical reflection on the topics.

name: Money and Banking I　０１
teacher: ヘンニガン　ペイン
summary_excerpt: This course provides a foundational understanding of monetary theory, fina......
summary: This course provides a foundational understanding of monetary theory, financial markets, and the banking system. We begin by analyzing the definitions of money, the mechanisms of money supply and demand, and the implementation of monetary policy by central banks. We then transition to financial markets, examining the valuation of bonds and stocks, before exploring the critical role of financial intermediaries. The course concludes with an analysis of financial crises and the challenges of monetary policy at the Zero Lower Bound (ZLB), linking theoretical frameworks to historical and contemporary economic events.
goal: Students completing this course will be familiar with 1) the fundamental theories of money supply, demand, and monetary policy and 2) the valuation of financial assets and the mechanics of banking crises. This class is targeted to 2nd-year undergraduate students or above.
study_outside: Before class, read the assigned textbook sections (60-90 mins). Review consists of completing custom practice problems analyzed during lectures (60 mins). This course prepares students for Money and Banking II."
schedule_plan:
1:
第１回　Money Supply
Introduction to the functions of money and monetary aggregates (M1, M2). Analysis of the central bank balance sheet and the multiple deposit creation process.
2:
第２回　Money Demand
Examination of the Quantity Theory of Money and Liquidity Preference Theory. Discussion on how interest rates and income levels determine the demand for real money balances.
3:
第３回　Monetary Policy Implementation
Overview of the central bank's policy toolkit, including Open Market Operations, discount lending, and reserve requirements. Discussion on how central banks target specific interest rates (e.g., Federal Funds Rate).
4:
第４回　Monetary Policy and Macro Fluctuations I
Introduction to the IS-LM framework. Analysis of how monetary policy shifts the LM curve and influences aggregate demand in the short run.
5:
第５回　Monetary Policy and Macro Fluctuations II
Extension of the IS-LM model to the Aggregate Demand-Aggregate Supply (AD-AS) framework. Analysis of inflation dynamics and the long-run neutrality of money.
6:
第６回　Midterm Review
In-class practice
7:
第７回　Midterm
In-class written examination covering the first half of the semester.
8:
第８回　Bonds
The economics of fixed-income securities. Analysis of bond pricing, yield-to-maturity calculations, and the Term Structure of Interest Rates (Yield Curve).
9:
第９回　Stocks
The economics of equity markets. Examination of the One-Period Valuation Model, the Gordon Growth Model, and the theory of Rational Expectations in financial markets.
10:
第１０回　Financial Intermediation
Analysis of the role of banks in the economy. Discussion on how financial intermediaries reduce transaction costs and mitigate asymmetric information problems (adverse selection and moral hazard).
11:
第１１回　Financial Crisis and ZLB I
Anatomy of a financial crisis. Discussion on asset price bubbles, banking panics, deleveraging, and the feedback loops that lead to deep recessions.
12:
第１２回　Financial Crisis and ZLB II
Monetary policy in the aftermath of a crisis. Analysis of the Liquidity Trap, the Zero Lower Bound (ZLB) constraint, and unconventional tools such as Quantitative Easing (QE).
13:
第１３回　Final Exam Review
Comprehensive review of the course.
14:
第１４回　Final Exam
Comprehensive final examination covering all course material, with an emphasis on the second half of the semester.

summary_excerpt: A defining characteristic of this course is its consistent use of a micro-......
summary: A defining characteristic of this course is its consistent use of a micro-founded, optimizing, dynamic general equilibrium framework throughout. The same core analytical structure is maintained across all chapters: we begin with a baseline model and then introduce targeted extensions to address each major topic in open-economy macroeconomics. Using this unified approach, the course studies the determinants of the current account in both small and large economies; adjustment dynamics following temporary, permanent, and anticipated shocks; the determination of the real exchange rate; the implications of fixed versus flexible exchange-rate regimes in the presence of nominal rigidities; interactions between monetary and fiscal policy; the role of capital controls when financial frictions are present; and the mechanisms underlying balance-of-payments crises.
goal: This course aims to present undergraduate and master's students an analysis of questions relevant for economic policy using the same basic analytical approach as is employed in the research literature.
study_outside: The prerequisites for this course are an introductory course in microeconomics and and more importantly one in macroeconomics. Although not very formalized (I will mostly use graphs to explain theoretical mechanisms), this course will use some basic mathematical tools that are common in any modern economic course. Students are required to attend regularly and participate actively.

name: Industrial Organization　０１
summary_excerpt: Industrial organization (IO) is a branch of microeconomics that studies ho......
summary:
Industrial organization (IO) is a branch of microeconomics that studies how firms compete with each other in markets or industries and the implications of competition on consumers and social welfare. Beyond the scope of basic microeconomics, IO studies the following situations:
(1) there are only a few firms in the market so that the strategic interaction between these firms is important, and
(2) firms can choose their strategy other than prices and productions, including product quality, advertisement, entry/exit, merger with other competitors, and innovation/R&D.
IO is strongly related to business/management strategy as well as public policies (regulation and competition policy). Although I put an emphasis on the theoretical aspects of IO, I will introduce real-world examples and empirical studies to demonstrate how IO theories can be used.
goal: The students (1) understand how to apply the theory of IO to analyze the behavior of firms in markets, and (2) understand the role of regulation and competition policy to improve marketoutcomes and welfare in oligopolistic markets.
study_outside: Students must have taken the following three courses that are required for the 1st year English-Degree Program students. (1) introduction to microeconomics, (2) Introduction to mathematical analysis, and (3) Introduction to game theory. Taking Microeconomics A/B and Game theory for the 2nd year and above are strongly recommended but not mandatory.

name: International Organization　０１
summary_excerpt: How and why were international organizations created/formed and sometimes ......
summary:
How and why were international organizations created/formed and sometimes collapsed? How and why do sovereign states agree to create international institutions and organizations? What has been the political dynamism behind any international organization? As an academic discipline, International Relations (IR) has attempted to answer those questions.
Through a longer history of international society, or society of sovereign states, the so-called international organizations were not naturally created. This course will look back the history of Western international society and its global expansion. It will then put such international organizations as the League of Nations and the United Nations (UN) in this historical context. It will particularly focus on the role of Japan in any international organization.
goal: This course will introduce students to the theory and history of international organization, and help them understand the following four subjects: (1) International Society, the English School or Rationalism as the third paradigm of International Relations IIR) in contrast to Realism and Liberalism, (2) the historic developments of Western international society and international organization, (3) the political dynamism behind the creation of the League of Nations and the United Nations, and (4) the historic significance of a global liberal order and the future of the 'West'.

You are strongly required to attend the lectures and/or watch the recorded lectures during the designated period. A frequent visit to Waseda Moodle is necessary for this course. You may be asked to write a short essay or answer a quiz in this course.

summary_excerpt: The course is concerned with the politics of European integration, focusin......
subtitle: Governance and politics of the European Union
summary:
The course is concerned with the politics of European integration, focusing on the governance of the European Union (EU). In order to advance high-level cooperation in various policy fields, the EU has developed a highly institutionalized system of governance and in the face of recent crises, it has further reformed its governance system and aimed at policy innovations in the relevant fields. Given the EU’s unprecedented level of institutional and policy development, this course addresses the following three main questions:
-      How have the institutional structure and public policies of the EC/EU developed over time since its inception in the1950s?
-      What factors are considered to have contributed to the development of the governance system and policies?
-      How has the EU reformed its governance system and policies in response to such recent crises, as the Eurozone crisis, the refugee/migration crisis, Brexit, global warming, the Covid-19 crisis and the Ukraine crisis?
With these questions in mind, this course aims to deepen our understanding of the evolution of the governance system of the EU. In the early phase of this course, students will aim to acquire a basic understanding of the EU, with focus on its history, institutions, policies and enlargement. In the middle phase, they will focus on main theories of European integration and consider various factors which are considered to have contributed to the advancement of European integration at different points. In the last phase, they will deal with the recent EU crises and consider why the crises occurred and how the EU has been responding to them.

summary:
The primary purpose of the course is to introduce students to a variety of concepts and theories to analyze global governance, with a focus on organizations and institutions including international and regional organizations, firms, and NGOs. Students will read materials not only from international relations but also from political science, economics, sociology, and anthropology. goal: Students will be exposed to a wide range of conceptual tools to analyze organizations and institutions. They will also learn how to conduct research on global governance, employing one or more of those tools. This is a seminar course, and all the students are expected to contribute to the class through discussion and presentation. They are also expected to submit a research proposal on topics of their choice.
