summary_excerpt: Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains re......
subtitle: Research Design in Comparative Politics
summary:
Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains relationships between social, economic and political variables while focusing on politics within countries. Comparison is a defining feature of the subfield, and a key component in scientific study more generally. Thus, comparative politics uses cross-national comparisons (as well as comparisons of change over time) to understand why political systems are free or not free, stable or unstable, violent or peaceful, stagnant or productive, etc.
This seminar will be conducted as a research and writing workshop. Previously, in Advanced Seminars 1 & 2, seminar participants gained familiarity with current research in comparative politics. Then, in Advanced Seminar 3, students learned how to design their own research projects in comparative politics.  In this seminar, students will now put their knowledge and research skills into practice.  The goal is for each of the seminar participants to complete a thesis project that will ultimately offer an original contribution to the subfield of comparative politics. The students will refine their research questions, clarify their theoretical arguments, and obtain empirical evidence. During the course of the semester, students will present their work in progress and offer constructive critiques of others’ work.
In principle, students should register concurrently in “Thesis.”
goal: * Students will develop practical skills in conducting research in comparative politics, including how to formulate research questions and how to develop and empirically test hypotheses using cross-national comparisons.
study_outside:
Students are expected to make weekly progress on their thesis project.
(Seminar students electing not to write a thesis will write a research paper on a topic of their choosing. This paper should be an empirical paper – that is, it should involve the analysis of evidence, either quantitative or qualitative, to evaluate a hypothesis. Just like the thesis writers, these students will be expected to share their work in progress during the semester, give a final presentation, and submit their final paper at the end of the semester. The paper should be at least 1500 words.)

summary_excerpt: Topics for the final semester of the advanced seminar series will be deter......
subtitle: Research Design in Comparative Politics
summary:
Comparative politics is the subfield of political science that explains relationships between social, economic and political variables while focusing on politics within countries. Comparison is a defining feature of the subfield, and a key component in scientific study more generally. Thus, comparative politics uses cross-national comparisons (as well as comparisons of change over time) to understand why political systems are free or not free, stable or unstable, violent or peaceful, stagnant or productive, etc.
This seminar will be conducted as a research and writing workshop. Previously, in Advanced Seminars 1 & 2, seminar participants gained familiarity with current research in comparative politics. Then, in Advanced Seminar 3, students learned how to design their own research projects in comparative politics.  In this seminar, students will now put their knowledge and research skills into practice.  The goal is for each of the seminar participants to complete a thesis project that will ultimately offer an original contribution to the subfield of comparative politics. The students will refine their research questions, clarify their theoretical arguments, and obtain empirical evidence. During the course of the semester, students will present their work in progress and offer constructive critiques of others’ work.
In principle, students should register concurrently in “Thesis.”
goal: * Students will develop practical skills in conducting research in comparative politics, including how to formulate research questions and how to develop and empirically test hypotheses using cross-national comparisons.
study_outside:
Students are expected to make weekly progress on their thesis project.
(Seminar students electing not to write a thesis will write a research paper on a topic of their choosing. This paper should be an empirical paper – that is, it should involve the analysis of evidence, either quantitative or qualitative, to evaluate a hypothesis. Just like the thesis writers, these students will be expected to share their work in progress during the semester, give a final presentation, and submit their final paper at the end of the semester. The paper should be at least 1500 words.)

name: Advanced Seminar IV　１４
summary_excerpt: Social data science is an emerging academic field where researchers use st......
subtitle: Social Data Science / Political Methodology
summary:
Social data science is an emerging academic field where researchers use statistics and programming to analyze or change society. Key is to understand human beings and their interactions behind data.
Political methodology is a subfield of political science focused on the development of quantitative tools for empirical political analysis. A relative of econometrics, psychometrics, biostatistics, etc., it is the "stats division" of political science.
If you liked Statistics I/II and want to learn more techniques for scientifically analyzing politics, policies, and society, this seminar will be a good fit for you.
This course is the second half of the two-year seminar sequence designed to train you as a social data scientist / political methodologist. Being trained as a political methodologist will make you a perfect candidate for a data scientist at a tech company, as well as a graduate program in political science focused on quantitative analysis (either at Waseda or abroad).
During the second year of the sequence, you will work on your own project. The project can be a research project (typically leading to a graduation thesis), a programming project (e.g. writing a software package), or a social implementation project (e.g. creating an app or a web service). You can work either on a solo project or as a group.
goal: The goal of the second-year seminar is for you to implement the skills you have developed over the past years you spent at Waseda and produce something original that embodies your intellectual creativity. You will decide an a specific project after the first class session in consultation with the professor and the other seminar participants.
study_outside: Each week, you will work on assignments related to your own project. Required hours will vary from week to week, but you should expect to spend 2-4 hours on those.

summary: This course teaches the theory of political economics, a recently growing area in the field of economics, in which economic theory and game theory are applied to understand political-economic phenomena. 1:
Introduction
What is political economics?
2:
Review of microeconomics
The invisible hand theorem, the utility frontier, and the first fundamental theorem of welfare economics are reviewed
3:
The theory of the second best and the social welfare function
The second fundamental theorem of welfare economics, the social welfare function, and the second-best optimal allocation are explained.
4:
Rational choice
The theory of preference relations and the construction of utility functions are explained.
5:
Aggregation of individual preferences
Aggregation rules of individual preferences and the paradox of voting are discussed.
6:
Arrow's impossibility theorem
Arrow's impossibility theorem is explained.
7:
Government failure 1
Besley and Coate's definition of government failure is introduced and discussed.
8:
Government failure 2
When government failure occurs is discussed.
9:
Chicago versus Virginia
The controversy between Chicago and Virginia schools over government failure is introduced.
10:
The political Coase theorem
The Coase theorem is introduced, and its application to the political world, i.e., the political Coase theorem, is discussed.
11:
Electoral competition
The Downsian model and Wittman model of electoral competition are introduced.
12:
Political agency
We will discuss the political agency model and the model of performance voting.
13:
The role of electoral promises
We will discuss the role of electoral promises within a model of performance voting.

Special interest politics
We will discuss what a special interest group is and how it tries to exercise political influence. The common agency model is also introduced. We will also consider the role of elections in special interest politics.

summary_excerpt: This course is about what has variously been called public choice, politic......
subtitle: Formal Models of Politics
summary:
This course is about what has variously been called public choice, political economy, positive political theory, formal political analysis, and much else. Whatever one calls it, this course is about the analysis of political choices and strategies.  Analytical approaches to politics involve breaking an argument down into individual pieces and building up conclusions from those pieces.  As a practical matter, this is often done with the use of mathematics, especially, game theory.  Currently, game-theoretical analyses are important methods to understand politics.
This field is also important in economics to understand how policies are decided and how to implement good policies. In some courses such as Microeconomics or Public Economics, you may learn about "market failures" such as oligopolistic markets, externalities or public goods. In the case of market failures, market mechanisms cannot achieve efficient outcomes, so the government needs to intervene to the market to solve these problems. To analyze these problems, we usually assume that the government acts in the public interest, i.e., the government can try to improve the lives of its citizens and implement the best policy for them. However, public servants are the same person as the rest of us. They prefer to pursue self-interest and may not be motivated by a higher calling. We will analyze such strategic behavior in both democratic and nondemocratic institutions, exploring how politicians, citizens, and other strategic actors behave in particular institutional environments.
The prerequisite is Introduction to  Game Theory (ゲーム理論入門).  You can understand my lectures well if you already took Game Theory A (ゲーム理論), but it is not a prerequisite.
What is more important than any specific previous coursework is to have some degree of comfort with material presented in a formal (i.e. mathematical) fashion.

summary_excerpt: This course will introduce fundamental definitions and concepts in linear ......
summary: This course will introduce fundamental definitions and concepts in linear algebra, beginning with vector spaces, linear maps and their representation by matrices. We will introduce the notions of determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and characteristic polynomials of matrices as required to state the Jordan Normal Form and Cayley-Hamilton theorems. Depending on time, we will also introduce inner product spaces and quadratic forms.
goal: This course aims to give students the mathematical vocabulary from linear algebra required to understand its applications to economics and econometrics. Rather than emphasizing computational methods, this course will focus on giving students experience in learning abstract mathematics and developing their mathematical maturity.
study_outside: Students are asked to read the lecture materials, and complete the exercises and examples which are given in class. There will be homework assignments set throughout the course, and students are also encouraged to try additional problems from the reference book.

summary_excerpt: This course is designed forpeople who want to become managers, human resou......
summary:
This course is designed forpeople who want to become managers, human resource professionals, orconsultants—people who really want to understand what drives performance andhow to bring people together effectively. This course is economics-based,which means that: (1) we assume that workers maximize their utility andemployers maximize their profit; (2) we analyze equilibria that arise as aresult of strategic interactions; and (3) our evaluation criterion fororganizations is “efficiency”.  The strength of economics is theability to conceptualize problems and provide clear prescriptions for problemsthat plague many managers.
This course is astrategy course, too. According to Michael Porter, strategy is creating fitamong a company’s activities. The typical question we ask during our casediscussion is what activities the firm should combine and how these activitiessupport its strategic position.
Topics includehiring, turnover, training, pay for performance, job assignment, tournament,seniority-based pay, evaluation, job design, teams, worker empowerment, gendergap, coordination, internal structure of the firm, etc.. In order to applyeconomics concepts to these topics, the course will use human capital theory,game theory, and contract theory. There are no prerequisites, but knowledge ofMicroeconomics B and Labor Economics I,II will help.
goal:
The students will be trained to be able to answer three key questions:
(1) How to motivate people, how to provide incentives?
The course will teach you how to motivate employees in ways that match business and job characteristics and further your organization’s objectives. It is important for all managers to understand the incentive aspect of compensation, job design, teams and employee participation.
(2) How to attract good people, or desired type of people to your firm?
HR strategy is path-dependent in the sense that what you have done in the past determines the quality and nature of current workforce you employ and the current workforce constrains what you can do today. Therefore, when considering the introduction of or changes in some practices, you need to think about what impacts these new policies will have on hiring or retention of employees.
(3) What organizational structure and HR systems induce the most efficient resource allocation? How can we collect and aggregate useful information to make right decisions?
Organization structure and job design affect the way information is collected, transmitted, and used within organization. Organizations that are good at adapting to gradual external changes may do poorly in coordinating decisions to deal with disruptive environmental changes. Organizations that are good at exploring new ways of creating values may fail to exploit many small opportunities to improve processes. Managers need to make delicate tradeoffs in designing organizations.
By discussing these questions in different contexts and using different tools, students will learn how to design and implement new practices and policies to improve firm performance.

You will be required to answer quizzes during each class session. Be sure to review the fundamental concepts after the class.
Also, when assigned reading is designated for class, come prepared to discuss its content.

summary_excerpt: This course provides an introduction to comparative political economy, the......
summary:
This course provides an introduction to comparative political economy, the study of how political and economic systems interact and vary across countries. It begins with classical debates on capitalism and the role of the state, then develops institutional approaches to comparing national models of capitalism, including varieties of capitalism, institutional change, and growth strategies. The course also examines democracy, welfare states, inequality, and the political constraints on reform. It concludes by applying these frameworks to contemporary challenges and reflecting on the strengths and limits of political economy models.
Some of the key questions we will touch on are: Why do capitalist economies differ across countries? How do democracy, inequality, and growth interact? What roles do interests, institutions, and ideas play in shaping economic policy and outcomes?
goal: First, it introduces students to the core concepts and analytical frameworks of comparative political economy, emphasizing the reciprocal relationship between states, markets, and societies.
study_outside: Students are expected to complete assigned readings and prepare in advance of each lecture.

This session will introduce the course and the subject of comparative political economy.
2:
第２回　Classical Political Economy (1): Smith and Marx
The big questions on capitalism and the state originate in the classical works of Adam Smith and Karl Marx. Early political economy framed capitalism asa system of production and distribution shaped by power and conflict, not just efficiency.
3:
第３回　Classical Political Economy (2): Hayek and Keynes
Twentieth-century debates focused on whether markets can self-regulateor require active state intervention to manage instability.
4:
第４回　Classical Political Economy (3): Polanyi, Schumpeter, and Friedman
Capitalism is neither static nor self-contained but evolves through political reactions, innovation, and ideological contestation.
5:
第５回　Institutions, Interests, and Coalitions
Economic outcomes depend on institutions that reflect past political compromises between social and economic interests.
6:
第６回　Varieties of Capitalism
Advanced capitalist economies organize firms, labor, finance, andwelfare in systematically different ways that shape economic performance.
7:
第７回　Institutional Change and the Limits of Ideal Types
How do capitalist institutions change over time, and why do they not simplyconverge?
8:
第８回　Growth Models and Production Regimes
Countries pursue different growth strategies that generate distinct political coalitions and distributional conflicts.
9:
第９回　Capitalism and Democracy
Economic institutions influence democratic stability, political representation, and long-term development paths.
10:
第１０回　Inequality, Welfare States, and Growth
Welfare states are not just redistributive but also shape economic performance and social risk-sharing.
11:
第１１回　Interests, Collective Action, and Power
Economic policy outcomes are shaped by conflicts between social groups whose ability to organize and influence politics varies systematically.
12:
第１２回　The Role of the State in Capitalist Economies
Capitalist economies rely on the state to regulate markets, stabilize growth, and manage distributional conflict, but states differ in how theyperform these functions.
13:
第１３回　Contemporary Challenges
Current challenges such as climate change or platform capitalism testwhether existing institutional frameworks can address twenty-first-century challenges.
14:
第１４回　Comparative Political Economy Revisited
The course concludes by revisiting major frameworks and assessing theirstrengths, limits, and practical relevance.

subtitle: A Lecture on John Rawls's Liberalism
summary:
John Rawls is widely regarded as the most important theorist in contemporary political theory. In this class, we will discuss his extensive theory in its entirety, paying close attention to his early and later works, as well as his magnum opus,
A Theory of Justice
(1971). In particular, we will closely examine his "political turn" in the 1980s and beyond.
goal:
(1) Understand the basic methods and orientations of contemporary analytical political theory.
(2) Acquire a comprehensive view on John Rawls's political theory.
study_outside: All students are expected to read the handouts distributed before each session. Afterwards, it is recommended that they study the books and articles introduced in the lecture and review the handouts.
schedule_plan:
1:
Introduction: Can Liberalism Survive in the 21st Century?
We will discuss a sweeping critique of modern liberalism by Patrick Deneen and a spirited defense of Rawlsian liberal egalitarianism by Daniel Chandler. Through this discussion, we will justify the major premises of this lecture: liberalism still matters and deserves serious consideration in the 21st century.
2:
John Rawls: A 20th-century Political Theorist
We will discuss the development of Rawls's political theory in the context of 20th-century philosophical trends and political events.
3:
Justice as Fairness (1): Rawls's Fundamental Ideas
We will introduce the fundamental ideas that constitute Rawls's theory, including social cooperation, the moral person, and the basic structure of society.
4:
Justice as Fairness (2): The Two Principles of Justice
We will discuss Rawls's two principles of justice, which include the principle of equal basic liberties, the principle of fair equality of opportunity, and the difference principle.
5:
Justice as Fairness (3): The Original Position
We will discuss the original position, which is a thought experiment introduced by Rawls to justify his principles of justice.
6:
Justice as Fairness (4): Rawls's Critique of Utilitarianism
We will examine the thorough and trenchant criticism of utilitarianism presented in
A Theory of Justice
, emphasizing the differences between utilitarianism and Rawls's perspective.
7:
Justice as Fairness (5): The Difference Principle and the Principle of Restricted Utility.
We will discuss Rawls's later, more ambiguous view on utilitarianism, which was developed in
Political Liberalism
and
Justice as Fairness: A Restatement
.
8:
Justice as Fairness (6): The Property-Owning Democracy
We will discuss the idea of property-owning democracy, which Ralws proposed as an institutional framework that satisfies the two principles of justice.
9:
Political Liberalism (1): The Problem of Stability
We will examine Rawls's discussion of the stability of the well-ordered society in the third part of
A Theory of Justice
, a failure of which he claimed prompted his political turn.
10:
Political Liberalism (2): The Idea of Overlapping Consensus
We will discuss major ideas that are characteristic of political liberalism, including the fact of reasonable pluralism, the liberal principle of legitimacy, and the overlapping consensus.
11:
Political Liberalism (3): The Idea of Public Reason
We will discuss Rawls's controversial claims about public reason, as presented in his final works, including "The Idea of Public Reason Revisited".
12:
The Law of Peoples
We will attempt to understand the many problematic arguments in
The Law of Peoples
by situating them within the context of his entire theory.努める。
13:
Reflective Equilibrium
We will propose an interpretation that Rawls' mature theory was an attempt at a general and wide reflective equilibrium in well-ordered liberal society, which is considered a realistic utopia.
14:
Summary and Discussion
There will be an opportunity for class discussion as long as time permits. If we fall behind schedule, we will have a regular lecture session.

summary_excerpt: Social and political life is not possible without the existence of certain......
subtitle: Contemporary Approaches to the Social Contract
summary: Social and political life is not possible without the existence of certain common rules or principles. However, what should the content of these rules or principles be, and why should people follow them? In this course, we will approach this question through the lens of normative political philosophy: in particular, by drawing on the insights of modern social contract theory. Roughly, social contract theorists hold that the fundamental rules or principles of society must be such that they are rationally acceptable to each and every individual. This attractive but vague ideal can be fleshed out in a variety of ways, depending on how we understand the related ideas of rationality, personhood, and society. This course will aim to provide students with an overview of these different approaches to the social contract by reading a selection of primary and secondary sources. We will also examine and evaluate contemporary criticisms of the social contract approach by other traditions, such as feminist philosophy.
goal:
1. To understand the characteristics of social contract theory and its significance for political thought.
2. To understand and critically evaluate the different versions of contemporary theories of the social contract.
3. To familiarize oneself with the basic methods of normative political philosophy, including identifying, critically assessing, and developing arguments.

summary: In this course, we examine the role of institutions in economic development from a comparative historical perspective and explore the causes and consequences of institutional change and persistence. Topics covered include economic, legal, political, and social institutions, such as firms, property rights, democracy, family, and public health. The details of course schedule and organization are subject to change depending on the number and composition of students.

summary_excerpt: Development economics is a relatively new field, originated in decoloniz......
subtitle: Economic Development in Globalization and Deglobalization
summary:
Development economics is a relatively new field, originated in decolonization after the World WarⅡ, and is unique in certain aspects. First, the study tends to be interdisciplinary, for the poverty and inequality often have different structural background unobserved in the mature economies. Second, since the poverty and other complexed problems need solution and right policy approaches, and as the analytical tools are developed, it has become a typical policy science with empirical evidences. Third, present development is substantially influenced by globalization and as the results, by external shocks sometimes in bigger frequency, unlike the experiences of most matured economies.
This class covers the leading issues in economic development for social science students, promoting balanced understanding based on theories and empirical researches. Starting from the basic understanding on povery, inequality and economic growth, this class focues more on international issues that less developed economies face in contemporary period, such as trade, foreign direct investment, balance of payment crisis, and, sustainabality, as well as other policy issues.
goal: The goal in this class is to get basic understanding why many less develped and even emerging econonies find it difficult to realize steady growth while reducing poverty and inequality, focusing on the chances and challenges coming from globalization. Upon the turbulent changes in the global trading system in recent years, negative impacts coming out of deglobalization are added.
study_outside: In each class, major references are provided and students are often assigned to read and present the contents to lead the class discussions.
schedule_plan:
1:
Class orientation: Development economics as an applied field
Development economnics deals with broad issues unique in less developed economies. The first class reviews the hisotry of this discipline briefly, and then discuss its interdisciplinary character, including the relations with development studies and international economics.
2:
Poverty
Poverty exists even in high income economies, but development economics has focused on the structrual chracter of the poverty unique in less developed or emerging economies. Starting with how to measure poverty, this sessopm deals with the policy responses for poverty reduction.
3:
Inequality
Less developed and emerging economies suffers not only from poverty but often more from inequality especially in globalization. This session discusses traditional and new structures for inequality in globalization.
4:
Economic growth (1)
Growth is naturally the major concerns for the less developed and emerging economies, but the implications from the growth theories may differ depending on their assuptions and how they see the constraints. Basic reviews are provided in this session, including Solow model and Endogenous growth theory.
5:
Economic growth (2)
Following the two classic model, this session tries to complenet the traditional model by structuralists' views shaping the historical perspectives.
6:
Trade theories and development
Fear for globalization in less developed and emerging economies starts when how to participate international trade is discussed. This session introduces theoretical and emperical grounds why trade participation works for development, including trade regime in globalization.
7:
Traden nd industrialization theories
This session discusses two types of trade policies experimented by many less developed economies, such as import substitution and export orientation. The theoretical grounds and emperical results for the policies will be introduced.
8:
FDI and trade, technology spill-over and productivity
Recent international trade has been boosted by rapid growth of FDI and the intra-firm trade by multi-national enterprises. Attracting FDI has turned to be a powerful way to participate trade for less developed economies but the skepticism still remains. This session discusses the FDI policies to maximize the benefit for the host economies. Major benefit of FDI is technology transfer from foreign multi-nationals to local firms, so that this class also discusses why some economies could absorb technologies efficiently while others fail, including the host country policies.
9:
Exchange regime and development strategies
Exchange regime and its management can play a siginificant role in financial globalization. This session deals with the choice of exchange rate regime related to development strategies to discuss its potential risks for BoP crisis in recent years.
10:
Balance of payment crisis
Financial globalization has offered both the development opportunities and big challenges for the developing/emerging economies. This class deals with different types of crisis expereienced by developing/emergiig economies.
11:
Structural adjustment
Once hitted by BoP crisis, structural adejustment is inevitable but while small number of economies recover quickly and relatively well, many tend to stagnate structurally. This session deals with the structural adjusment program and the implementation process differentiating the returning paths for growth.
12:
Aid and development
Though the share of Official Development Aid (ODA) in capital flows to develpoping/emerging economies has shrunk substantially in along with financial globalization, the role only taken by aid exists especially for the crisis economies. Ths session deals with the changing role of aid in development.
13:
Institutions and development
Under the influence of new institutional economics, the institutional settings have been accounted as an important or even decisive factor for economic performance. Constantly challeged and innovated ideas on the role of government has helped shaping the discussion. This session tries to overviews what institutions and why and how the institutions are important for sustanbainable growth.
14:
Environment and development
While globalization continues to increase more competitive pressures for developing/emerging economies, they are also required to contribute to the sutainable growth, including green growth. This session discusses how the North and the South can cooperate together for the common goals.

summary_excerpt: In recent years, interest in text analysis within the social sciences has ......
summary:
In recent years, interest in text analysis within the social sciences has grown dramatically. This rise has been driven by the increasing availability of textual data and by new computational methods that enable researchers to draw substantively important inferences about politics and society from large collections of texts. This course provides students with the theoretical foundations and practical skills needed to analyze text data in social science research. It also offers an introduction to concepts and methods that underpin contemporary developments in artificial intelligence and large language models.
The course begins with the fundamentals of text representation, including text pre-processing and the bag-of-words approach. It then introduces a range of methods for extracting information from texts, moving from unsupervised approaches that discover latent themes in documents to supervised machine learning techniques that classify texts into predefined categories. Particular attention is devoted to the validation and interpretation of machine learning models. The course concludes with an introduction to static word embedding methods, focusing on how distributed representations of words can capture semantic relationships that go beyond traditional bag-of-words models.
The course focuses on four main areas:
1.Text representation and preprocessing. We examine how textual data can be transformed into structured data suitable for quantitative analysis, with particular attention to the bag-of-words framework.
2.Unsupervised text classification. We introduce topic modeling techniques, which are used to uncover latent themes and issue dimensions in large collections of texts.
3.Supervised text classification. We discuss machine learning methods for categorizing texts into predefined classes. Topics include the dictionary approach, common classification algorithms such as naïve Bayes and random forests, model validation through cross-validation, and techniques for model interpretation.
4.Word embedding methods. We explore static word embedding techniques, with a particular focus on GloVe models, highlighting how they differ from traditional text representations and how they can be used to capture semantic relationships between words.
Lab sessions are a central component of the course and provide hands-on experience implementing the methods discussed in class using R. Students are expected to bring their own laptops with R, RStudio, and the required packages installed and functioning (installation instructions will be provided in advance).

summary:
This course introduces students to quantitative research methods in the social sciences. Students will learn to collect, process, and analyze real-world data using statistical tools, as well as gain an understanding of research design and causal inference. This will prepare students to conduct their own research projects. The course emphasizes practical application over mathematical derivations, making it accessible to students without an advanced math background.
Each class is divided into two parts: the first half will cover key concepts and methods, while the second half will focus on reviewing exercises and discussing their solutions. Students will also complete an independent research project, where they will formulate a research question, collect and analyze data, and summarize their findings. The project will be presented in class and submitted as a final report.

name: Population Economics ０１
summary_excerpt: We study the theoretical and empirical foundations of labor economics usin......
subtitle: Learning Labor Economics: Theory and Empirics
summary:
We study the theoretical and empirical foundations of labor economics using a globally recognized textbook. We explore the mechanisms and labor market impacts of various socioeconomic factors, including immigration, labor force participation, college enrollment, racial and gender discrimination, incentive pay systems, and labor unions. Building on these theoretical frameworks, we also discuss major policy issues such as the minimum wage, workplace safety regulations, and various taxes and subsidies.
Each week, I will introduce influential papers from different subfields. To facilitate a deeper understanding of empirical research, I will also provide guidance on causal inference and widely used empirical methods. I emphasize that studying labor economics serves as an important gateway to other empirical micro fields, including education, health, environmental, development, and urban economics.
goal: 1. Understand the mechanisms and labor market impacts of various socioeconomic factors, employing both mathematical and intuitive frameworks of labor economics.
study_outside: Basic knowledge of introductory microeconomics is required. Familiarity with causal inference or prior coursework in econometrics is an advantage. Programming is not required.
schedule_plan:
1:
Course Introduction (Chapter 1)
I start by introducing the field of labor economics. Then, I will briefly overview the concepts and tools of causal inference, essential for understanding modern empirical research.
2:
Labor supply (Chapter 2)
We learn the mechanics of the labor market, dividing into the supply side, the demand side and the competitive equilibrium. On Day 2, we learn a model of labor force participation both for individual and a couple together with a life-cycle model.
Examples
: Wages and sleep time, Labor supply after winning lotteries
Policies
: Disability benefits
3:
Labor demand (Chapter 3)
We learn the basic model of hiring decision of firms to derive a labor demand curve in the short run and long run. Then, we study the key concept of elasticity of substitution, which is also central to understand the expanding wage inequality.
Examples
: estimation of the labor demand curve by mobilization of men during the WW2
Policies
: California's overtime regulations, minimum wage
4:
Labor market equilibrium 1 (Chapter 4)
The equilibrium is determined by intersecting the demand and supply curves. We consider the concept of labor surplus and producer surplus, and economic welfare. Then, we examine policy issues by comparative statics. As an application of the demand-supply framework, we discuss the labor impact of immigration. I introduce the concept of  immigration surplus, developed by Borjas.
Examples
: The Intifadah and Palestian Wages; the impact of Hurricanes on the Labor Market; the Mariel Boatlifts
Policies
: Payroll taxes (subsidies) and Mandated benefits
5:
Labor market equilibrium 2 (Chapter 4) and Introduction to modern empirical economics
I continue a part of discussions in the previous week. I overview the state-of-the-art of applied micro economics (including labor economics).
6:
Economics of education (Chapter 6)
A worker differs in their skill, earned by human capital investment. We consider the determinants and impacts of education choice by a simple model. The role of signaling is discussed in contrast to the human capital theory. (This chapter serves as the basis for the economics of education.)
Examples:
Destiny at Age 6
Policies:
School construction in Indonesia
7:
Wage distribution (Chapter 7)
The wage inequality is expanding, but why? The debate is not finished yet, but we answer to this question by the labor demand framework. We also consider the inequality across generations.
Examples:
Earnings and substance abuse; the effect of computers on wage inequality
Policies:
Training programs
8:
Compensating wage differential (Chapter 5)
.Setting wages aside, jobs are different in many dimensions. Compensating wage differentials are wage difference based on the job amenities. For example, risky dangerous jobs offer higher wages to attract workers.
Examples:
Jumpers in Japan; the Computing the value of life from the speed deregulation
Policies:
Safety and health regulations; health insurance
9:
Labor mobility (Chapter 8)
Mobility across occupations, locations is a substantial decision making for individuals. We discuss the mechanism of domestic and international migration.
Examples:
Power couples; health insurance and job lock
10:
Incentive pay (Chapter 11)
Canonical payment system is based on hours worked, but many businesses adopt an incentive pay scheme based on measurable performances. We consider the impact of incentive pay in many occupations. (e.g. blue-collar workers, sports players)
Examples:
Windshields by the piece
Policies:
Incentive pay for CEOs and teachers
11:
Unemployment (Chapter 12)
Unemployment cannot be explained by a competitive equilibrium. A search model was developed to derive unemployment. We also discuss an unemployment insurance system as a national safety net.
Examples:
the effect of Graduating during a Recession; job finding via kinship
Policies:
Cash bonuses and Unemployment duration
12:
Labor unions (Chapter 10)
In the widening wealth gap between workers and capitalists, a new movement for building a union is underway. We review the history and decline of labor unions in the U.S. After that we learn the theory of labor unions, which augments the workers' split of the pie.
Examples:
the cost of labor disputes
Policies:
Public sector unions (e.g. teachers)
13:
Labor market discrimination (Chapter 9)
The society of diversity involves discrimination. We study the theory of discrimination with application to gender, race, ethnicity and disability. We also learn an empirical framework to detect discrimination.
Examples:
Does beauty pay?; Blind audition at the orchestra; Does tones of skin color matter for wages?
Policies:
The black-white wage gap; the male-female wage gap
14:
Final exam (in-class)
After the exam, I briefly review a part of controversial questions.

This textbook is excellent in terms of theoretical rigor and its interesting applications to the real world. In principle, each class covers one chapter. The class materials summarize the main contents, but I encourage participants to borrow or purchase the textbook.
